LAREDO, Texas — Nearly one in four Webb County residents — roughly 60,000 people — relies on SNAP food benefits. That’s more than double the statewide rate. And while benefits ticked up 2.9% this month through a cost-of-living adjustment, a far bigger story is unfolding underneath: the largest rollback of food assistance in modern history is about to hit the county’s poorest families.

This is who they are, what’s changing, and where to get help.

THE 60,000: A DEMOGRAPHIC PORTRAIT

Webb County’s SNAP population looks nothing like the national stereotype of the program — because Webb County looks nothing like the nation.

About 90 to 95 percent are Hispanic, in a county that is 95 percent Hispanic. The overwhelming majority — 95 percent of SNAP users nationally — are U.S. citizens.

Nearly four in ten are children: roughly 23,400 kids. About 12,000 are seniors over 60. Another 6,000 are disabled. Almost eight in ten recipient households include a child, an elderly person, or someone with a disability.

They are the working poor. About a third of SNAP households have earned income — cashiers, cooks, drivers, sales clerks in Laredo’s trade, retail, and service economy. The mean wage in Laredo is $22.63 an hour versus $32.66 nationally; food preparation workers average $12.90, health care support $12.62. More than half of SNAP households with children have someone working. In a county where the median household income is $63,058 — against roughly $80,000 nationally — and 21.3 percent live below the poverty line, work alone doesn’t put food on the table.

They are less educated through no fault of their own: only 70.9 percent of Webb County adults hold a high school diploma (versus 89 percent nationally), and just 14 percent hold a bachelor’s degree (versus 36 percent).

Child poverty runs at 29 percent — some 24,160 children. Senior poverty is 24.6 percent. Even 6.6 percent of full-time workers live below the poverty line.

THE CLIFF

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed July 4, 2025, is gutting SNAP eligibility even as the cost-of-living bump adds about $29 a month for a family of four (maximum benefit $994 to $1,023). The Congressional Budget Office estimates $186 billion in cuts through 2034, removing about 2.4 million people in a typical month. More than 4 million have already left the program nationally.

The new rules: work requirements expanded to ages 18–64 (up from 18–54) — 80 hours a month or benefits end after three months. Exemptions eliminated for veterans, homeless individuals, and former foster youth. Parents are only exempt with a child under 14 (down from under 18). Geographic waivers now require unemployment above 10 percent — Webb County sits at 4.4 percent, so no waiver. Non-citizen eligibility narrowed.

Texas is already collapsing: 3.47 million recipients in fiscal 2025 down to 2.81 million by June 2026 — a 16 percent drop, some 550,000 people, more than half of them children. Webb County’s 60,000 is not a record — it’s the post-attrition number. An estimated 11,400 more county residents are at risk of losing benefits entirely under the new rules.

The cruelest twist: the 80-hour-a-month documentation rule hits irregular-schedule retail, food service, and warehouse workers hardest — exactly Webb County’s workforce. And Texas sat out Summer EBT for the third straight summer, forfeiting $120 per child in summer grocery benefits.

Deportation fears are also driving mixed-status families off the rolls voluntarily — a chilling effect no statute required.

CAN ANYONE ABSORB THIS?

No. The South Texas Food Bank distributed 22 million pounds across eight counties in 2026 — and Feeding Texas reports the statistic that ends the argument: SNAP provides nine meals for every one meal a food bank can supply. Calls to 211 for food assistance are up 28.6 percent; pantry referrals up 37 percent. Demand is at record highs while enrollment falls.

Meals on Wheels in Laredo serves more than 90,000 meals a year from a new $1.5 million facility — and still carries a 250-person waitlist.

THE HEALTH STAKES

Webb County’s adult diabetes rate is 18 percent — 16th highest in Texas, six points above the state average. When benefits shrink, families buy the cheapest calories available. The cuts will worsen the exact food-related illness already devastating the county.

WHERE TO GET HELP IN WEBB COUNTY

If you or someone you know needs food, these are verified local resources. Call ahead — hours can change.

South Texas Food Bank — 2121 Jefferson St, Laredo, (956) 726-3120. Main food bank for the region; mobile pantries and partner agencies across the county.

Catholic Charities of Laredo — food assistance programs; call (956) 727-2143.

Bethany House of Laredo — 817 Salinas Ave, (956) 722-4152. Meals and services.

Salvation Army Laredo — 408 S. Stone Ave, (956) 723-5451. Food pantry and assistance.

St. Vincent de Paul — parish-based assistance; contact local Catholic parishes.

Laredo Meals on Wheels — senior home-delivered meals; 250-person waitlist as of March 2026, apply early.

WIC (Women, Infants and Children) — Texas WIC clinics in Laredo; for pregnant women and children under 5.

LISD Community Eligibility Provision — free meals for ALL students, 2026–27 school year, no application needed.

Texas 211 — dial 2-1-1 for referrals to food pantries, including church-based distributions.

Church food pantries operate across Laredo and the colonias — including distributions in El Cenizo, Rio Bravo, and La Presa, where community centers double as food distribution points. Ask your parish or call 211 for the current schedule.

Veterans in need: contact the Webb County Veterans Service Office.
